12122:
I've gathered some files together for my first uploads to the FTP server for the new year.  These come from a variety of sources, now including Richard Houser's tape collection (courtesy of Lance).  Highlights include what I believe is the earliest Dungeons & Dragons utility for the Astrocade--a set of four programs by Guy McLimore released in 1979.  I've also sorted through the rest of the Rich Tietjens tapes I have and have gotten a few more programs.  Many programs by Mark Keller previously only available as type-in scans are now archived as .wav files.  Most of Mark Keller's programs include version numbers.  It's generally unclear how many versions of his programs were actually released.  And for those with a RAM expansion, I've now got the extra RAM version of Quadra by Mike White.  So, this actually marks quite a few programs off the list.

I have at this point recorded most of the tapes that I know of, though I still haven't looked at many of the recordings.  I'm really running out of commercial programs to archive.  There are some utilities for the Blue RAM that I mostly can't even use (who actually has an Astrocade modem?).  Then all I can really think of is the 300 baud versions of some programs already archived in 2000 baud format.  So, if anyone knows where to find the lost programs, please speak up.  I'll continue to archive the utilities, prototypes, and newsletter programs for the moment as time allows.

Also included are scans of a couple of WaveMakers tapes that Jack Flynn loaned me.

See below for full notes on the files.

AstroBASIC:
COH (198x)(possibly Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto).zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "New Game COH".  The reverse of the tape had a number of newsletter programs, plus a prototype of Laser Fortress by Ken Lill.  This game is clearly incomplete.  You can move a robot sprite around the screen, and it flashes when you run into some background elements, but that's all.

COH (198x)(possibly Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a].zip -  found on same tape as COH (proto).  Whereas before the top two robots were just background elements, now they can be controlled by player 2.  Pushing left and right on the joystick moves the left character left and right, while pushing up and down on the joystick moves the right character left and right.  It's still incomplete.


COH (198x)(possibly Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a2].zip - found on same tape as COH (proto) and (proto)[a].  This version changes the background some, but now nothing in controllable.

COH (198x)(possibly Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a3].zip - found on same tape as COH (proto) through (proto)[a2].  Seems the same as (proto)[a2].

COH (198x)(possibly Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a4].zip - found on same tape as COH (proto) through (proto)[a2].  Seems the same as (proto)[a2] and (proto)[a3].

Connect Four (1980)(Robert Leake)(2000 baud).zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "New Game COH".  It's a Cursor program.  The first few lines are machine language.

Connect Four Parameter Program (1980)(Robert Leake and Fred Cornett)(2000 baud).zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "New Game COH".  It's a Cursor program.  It helps the user enter the machine language portion of the Connect Four code.

Frustration Fortress (198x)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a12].zip,
Frustration Fortress (198x)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a13].zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "New Game COH".  They both crash when run.

Galactibattle (1980)(Brett W. Lathrope and Fred Cornett)(2000 baud).zip - Cursor program found in Ken Lill's tape collection.

Laser Fortress (198x)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto).zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled simply "Games".  This was eventually printed in The Arcadian as Frustration Fortress, but here, the title screen calls it Laser Fortress, Gambits Tape #1.

Quickdraw (1982)(New Image)(2000 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial tape in Richard Houser's collection.  This can replace the bad dump currently on-line.  It has a graphical title screen, unlike the alternate version I uploaded previously.

Riddle (1982)(New Image)(2000 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial tape in Richard Houser's collection.  This can replace the version currently on-line, which has some garbage on the title screen.


Bally BASIC:
23 Matches (1980)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud)[a].zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 15".

Alles Lookenspeepers (19xx)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 17".  Press any key to display letter written in a sort of German/English hybrid.

Biorhythm 3.0 (1980)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.

Blackjack II (1980)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.

Blackjack II (no comments) (1980)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - I made a version of the program with the comments removed to save space, as the comments themselves instruct.

Blockout 5.0 (1981)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - unpublished Arcadian submission found in Bob Fabris' tape collection.  It's a Breakout-style game.  The tape was missing a couple of lines, but I corrected it based on a note from Mark Keller found with Bob Fabris' documents.

Bombardment II 2.0 (1981)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.


Bullseye II 2.0 (1981)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.

Canary (19xx)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 6".  It plays a sound that resembles birdsong.

Cash Register (1980)(Rich Tietjens and John Eric)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 22".  Hold 1 to play change-making game.  The items and prices are encoded in the @() array.  Hold 2 to enter new items.  I haven't really figured out the controls for this option.  Hold 3 to view current array values.

Chase III 1.0 (1981)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.

Craps (1980)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 11". It prints out instructions before starting.

Dungeon Grafix I (1979)(Guy McLimore)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection.  Part of Dungeons & Dragons package advertised in Arcadian Volume 1, page 54.

Dungeon Grafix II (1979)(Guy McLimore)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection.  Part of Dungeons & Dragons package advertised in Arcadian Volume 1, page 54.

Fantasy People (1979)(Guy McLimore)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection.  Part of Dungeons & Dragons package advertised in Arcadian Volume 1, page 54.

Farenheit Celcius Conversion (19xx)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Richard Houser collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 5".  The line numbers are stored as words, so the .txt file looks a little confusing.

File Create (1980)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.

Hardcopy Converter Version 1 (19xx)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens". Load program with with ":INPUT".  It prints out brief instructions before loading the code.  This is a short utility to convert characters in a listing that may not work with a printer, such as changing the division sign to a forward slash.

Hardcopy Converter Version 2 (19xx)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens". Load program with with ":INPUT 2", or use ":INPUT 3" to load brief instructions after the program.  This is a short utility to convert characters in a listing that may not work with a printer, such as changing the division sign to a forward slash.  This version will automatically list the program when finished.

Keno II 2.0 (1981)(Mark Keller)(300 baud)(PD).zip - Arcadian program found in Bob Fabris collection on tape along with the unpublished programs Pinball I and Blockout 5.0.  I'd actually already found Keno II 2.0 on a different tape in the Bob Fabris collection.  I compared the two, and while the BASIC code is identical, the data in the @() array is completely different.  It turns out that the new one I'm uploading matches what was printed in the Arcadian.  So, I'm making this the primary version.  Please rename the file currently on this page:
http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/arcadian.html
to Keno II 2.0 (1981)(Mark Keller)(300 baud)(PD)[a]

Klingon Capture (1980)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Bob Fabris collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens". Load with ":INPUT 21".  It prints a letter from Starfleet Command before loading the program.  Use the joystick to move the Federation ship, and pull the trigger to destroy the sector it's currently in.  Try to surround the Klingon ship with destroyed sectors, but don't damage the ship itself.  The Klingon ship only rarely moves.

Life 3.0 (1980)(Mark Keller)(300 baud).zip - found on hand-labeled tape in Richard Houser's collection along with several other programs by Mark Keller.  See type-in program scan for instructions.

      I've gathered some files together for my first uploads to the FTP server for the new year.  These come from a variety of sources, now including Richard Houser's tape collection (courtesy of Lance).  Highlights include what I believe is the earliest Dungeons & Dragons utility for the Astrocade--a set of four programs by Guy McLimore released in 1979.  I've also sorted through the rest of the Rich Tietjens tapes I have and have gotten a few more programs.  Many programs by Mark Keller previously only available as type-in scans are now archived as .wav files.  Most of Mark Keller's programs include version numbers.  It's generally unclear how many versions of his programs were actually released.  And for those with a RAM expansion, I've now got the extra RAM version of Quadra by Mike
 White.  So, this actually marks quite a few programs off the list.
I have at this point recorded most of the tapes that I know of, though I still haven't looked at many of the recordings.  I'm really running out of commercial programs to archive.  There are some utilities for the Blue RAM that I mostly can't even use (who actually has an Astrocade modem?).  Then all I can really think of is the 300 baud versions of some programs already archived in 2000 baud format.  So, if anyone knows where to find the lost programs, please speak up.  I'll continue to archive the utilities, prototypes, and newsletter programs for the moment as time allows.
Also included are scans of a couple of WaveMakers tapes that Jack Flynn loaned me.

 was first advertised in the Fall 1980 Sourcebook.  On the tape, the program had the BASIC code first, then machine language code, then instructions printed out at the very end.  It then crashed on "CALL20200".  Richard Degler pointed out a problem with "the LIB starting at %(20180) which after 20 chars will overwrite the machine code at %(20200)".  Without changing any code or data, I modified it such that the instructions are first rather than last. Now it runs enough to sometimes complete a short game, but frequently crashes on line 32.  I haven't figured out what specifically triggers this.  Due to this bug, and the tape it was found on, I've decided to label it as a prototype version.  Hopefully the bug was fixed before the program was actually published.  The main program stores the line numbers as words.  I've included a text file that has the BASIC code with regular line numbers, which I got by listing
 it back into my computer.
Space War Instructions (1980)(Rich Tietjens)(300 baud).zip - found in Richard Houser collection on tape hand-labeled "Programs From Rich Tietjens".  Load with ":INPUT 4".  I believe Rich used this to write out the graphics data and instructions at the end of the Spacewar program located immediately before it on the tape.

12142:
I had pretty good luck with just a regular threshold, since the black ink is a lot darker than the red ink.  In GIMP, go to Colors/Threshold and select the threshold value.  I used 200.  Now, you have a black and white image without the overlay.  Go ahead and go to Image/Mode/Indexed and select "Use black and white (1 bit) palette" so it will actually save it as a much smaller binary image.  If you want better text quality, you might try scanning at 600dpi.  Does this work for you?

Paul

Box 4 contains 19 folders and the "Nutting Manual."  Everything in the folders has been scanned.  The "Nutting Manual" will be a work in progress and will be uploaded at a later date.  This list was created with the TREE command using the Windows XP command line.  Tree seems to get far less use than it should, so I'll just share this simple command:

TREE [drive:][path] [/F] [/A]

   /F   Display the names of the files in each folder.
   /A   Use ASCII instead of extended characters.

The output was directed to a file, like this: "tree /f /a > tree.txt."  This output listing is included in this document.

This listing contains every file that needed to be scanned.  Unlike the previous boxes, much less had to be scanned.  This isn't just because there were less documents in Box 4 (which there was), but also because some of the material had already been scanned and uploaded to the BallyAlley.com website.  All of the material was scanned in 300-dpi TIFF format.  A few of the files have been converted to pdf format so that I could share them with Paul (these pdf files are still present, but I will eventually delete them when I make high-quality pdfs of the TIFF that I sent to Paul).

Let me draw your attention to a few items:

1) Rabbit RX83 directory - This directory has a whole bunch of interesting material.  This RX83 computer was planned for release in the U.S., but it never came out.  I first asked about this computer back on Nov, 11, 2007 on DigitPress.com.  Weirdly, this posting that I made is the very first hit that comes up today in Google when I search for information about this computer.  Since this computer never was released, and there is still nearly nothing available about it, when I post this information to the BallyAlely website, then suddenly I'll have sort of a RabbitRX83Alley.com.  Some of the letters between Bob and the Rabbit company work out the details about converting Astrocade software to the Rabbit RX83.  Neat reading!

2) Z80 Minicourse - There are a few extra scans of this manual now.  One of them is lightly commented by the author of the minicourse-- which makes for some amusing reading in some of the areas where he picks on the material that he wrote.

3) R&L Enterprises - This folder has a better scan of the 64K RAM Board and a letter by, I think, Rusty (the letter is marked as from "Guess Who?"-- which isn't useful in archiving work!).

4) Viper - This contains a scan of a different (later?) version of the Viper 1 manual.  Certainly this version is longer than the one currently online which is marked "preliminary."  Lance may find this useful.  There is also a different glossy picture of the Viper that has the two built-in 5 1/4 disk drives and a keyboard (it's VERY similar to what's online already, but this is a glossy large print, so it probably has more details.).

5) BL-1200 - The "BL-1200" is the model number of, I think, The Home Library Computer.  There are two documents here.  One looks like a hacker tried to delve deeply into his computer and figure-out how it ticked.  The other is a preliminary version of the "BL-1200 User's Manual" (maybe by the same person that hacked their system).  Until I started scanning this folder, I had always thought that all of this material was about some sort of prototype.  It no longer appears that way to me at all.

6) Jameco Keyboard - Contains material that users came up with to hook up a Jameco 63-key keyboard to their Bally Arcade using the 300-Baud interface.

7) Mike White - This folder has material that I already made into a low-quality pdf and sent to Paul.  This is a manila envelope that contains Mike White's submission tape to Bob from 1982/83-ish.  The actual handwritten program listings are 54 pages long!  Yeah, 54 pages!  No wonder Mike finally got himself a printer!  The tape with the programs was also in the envelope (it's a nice TDK 60-minute tape in the case) and I'll be sending that tape off to Paul soon for archiving purposes.

8) List Formatter - This is a program that George Moses wrote that allowed a user to list and print a program to printer.  This version was specially modified for Bob Fabris' NEC printer.  This version would support the division sign and some other special characters.  George comments that only one byte was left free after he finished writing this program!

9) Folder 14 (Programs) - This folder contains nine program listings that are printed onto the silver (thermal?) paper that most of the Bally users with printers seemed to use back in the late seventies and early eighties.  All of these programs have been archived in one way or another, but one of particular note is "Sub Search" which has several listings (three, I think).  The listings of "Sub Search" are marked as Old, New and then there is one that is different and is marked up (a work in progress?).

There are many other folders that have various bits of information in them.  These other folders seemed to have been ones that I created myself when I first received the collection.  When I got the documentation of the Fabris Collection, most of the boxes still had folders which were organized, but some of it wasn't organized at all.  With a couple of boxes the folders had either opened previously or hadn't ever been organized.  I placed these documents into folders when I placed everything into hanging folders a few years ago.

The one item not included in this listing is the "Nutting Manual," which I'll scan in color and then reduce the threshold to get a better B&W copy than the version which is already online.  The online version has "Proprietary Information" on nearly every page.  Since this manual is already online, and will take some time to scan, I'll scan in pages when I get some free time here and there.  I'll be in no rush to finish it.  When I'm done, the text results should be nice, but that doesn't matter to me too much (since the manual was re-typed years ago).  What I'm most concerned about are the illustrations, which are quite helpful in understanding the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  I hope to have AT LEAST clean versions of these.

It is possible that the flaw you mentioned is related to the way Bally BASIC stores programs on tape. In case you have tried to print a program listing "saving it" to the printer, instead of recording it to tape, all BASIC commands have probably been printed as lowercase, single-character letters, making the listing appear wrong.

As far as I remember, this adaptation to the cartridge provided it with a serial output, so it could be connected to a suitable serial printer. Connecting to the PC would probably require the cable, a PC with a serial port (this is becoming rare, lately - I think my desktop computer still have one) and some sort of terminal program, like Hyperterminal, in order to "listen" to the program sent by the Astrocade. The serial port would have to be configured for 300-baud reception, of course.

I always wondered if the opposite would be possible (and it probably is): to adapt a cartridge to receive serial input, bypassing the cartridge analog filtering, and all, as it would be useful to transfer programs directly, flawlessly, from the PC to the Astrocade, without having to resort to complex audio manipulation tools. But, by now, I miss the required equipment to play with this myself.

Hey, you're program works great, Lance.  Your results look about identical to the TRS-80 Color Computer version.  There is a screenshot of the results of the CoCo program on page 54 of the book-- see how similar it looks?

Since the Astrocade (and other 8-bit computers) don't have access to the PET ASCII version of the / and \ that were used in the C64 version, there will be space between each letter and each line, thus the "maze" doesn't look as closed as it should.  I went ahead and used Photoshop to clean up the blank spaces below each line, and the maze can be seen MUCH more easily.

In order to simulate this program more effectively, some custom graphics would have to be used.  That's not covered in the BASIC manual, but of course it's covered in the Arcadian.  This would mean abandoning the one line and the simplicity of it all, but it could certainly be done!

I've attached three screenshots from MESS emulating the Astrocade and running this program:

1) 10 PRINT (Jan 2012)(Lance Squire)(One Line Program).gif - This is what Lance's program looks like when typed into AstroBASIC.

2) 10 PRINT (Jan 2012)(Lance Squire)(Program Results).gif - This is what the program looks like after it fills the screen.  Of course, the program will run forever and the "maze" will scroll up.

3) 10 PRINT (Jan 2012)(Lance Squire)(Modified Results).gif - This is a modified version of the above image.  It shows a closer approximation of Lance's program if no space were between each line from top to bottom (all the space ends up accumulating at the bottom of the screen, which looks pretty weird).

I've also included a save state of Lance's program, so you can run it if you have the latest version of MESS installed.  Here's how:

The file 1.sta is the save state of an AstroBASIC MESS program saved in slot one.  This short one line program is by Lance Squire and was written January 19, 2013.  It attempts to emulate the Commodore 64 "10 PRINT" program in the book "10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1));:GOTO 10."  Lance version looks like this:

10 @(1)=47;@(2)=92;TV=@(RND(2));GOTO 10

If you load this saved state into with MESSD 0.148, then it should load fine for you.  You can probably also load it just fine using the regular version of MESS 0.148.

In order to load the saved state, place it into your MAME directory (which holds MESS) under:

mame0148b_debug\sta\astrocde

If you already have a save state, and you overwrite it with this one, then you will lose your other save state, so be careful.

When you're ready to load the program, press F7 and choose slot 1.  The program should appear on the screen followed by a division sign.  Whenever I save an AstroBASIC state, a division sign is always typed on the screen and also saved.  I don't know why, but it doesn't interfere with anything.  Erase the division sign, type RUN and try the program out.  It's a neat little maze, isn't it?!?

Thanks to Lance for making a quick version of this program-- it was fun to see the quick turn-around time.

On a side note, does anyone know why I get these symbols on-screen when I reload a program (I recall Richard Degler mentioning it before-- but I can't remember a reason that he may have explained).

Some comments on the "10 PRINT" program when running under Blue Ram BASIC:

1) It looks more like the Commodore 64 version because the color scheme of Blue Ram BASIC is much more similar to that of the C64's native color of BASIC (dark blue and light blue vs. Black text on a white background).  Point to Blue Ram BASIC.

2) Blue Ram BASIC can display more characters on the screen both right to left and top to bottom than AstroBASIC is able to do.  This also includes more room at the bottom of the screen used by Blue Ram because it has access to more additional RAM and thus doesn't need to use screen RAM for main memory as AstroBASIC must do.  This combination makes all the lines appear tighter and thus the "maze" is easier to make out.  Also, there isn't as much space between the lines either vertically or horizontally, making the maze more "maze-like."  Point to Blue Ram BASIC.

3) Blue Ram BASIC's "maze" doesn't seem as random as the one create under AstroBASIC.  I find this odd since I imagined that both Astro and Blue Ram BASICs were using the on-board ROM random routine called "RANGED" (described on page 80 of the Nutting Manual) to get random numbers.  I ran the program several times in Blue Ram BASIC, and while the results were different each time, the randomness didn't seem to work as well as it did under AstroBASIC.  Perhaps it's just my perception of it.  Still, point to AstroBASIC.

I guess the next version of the program is the one I already mentioned: a version of "10 PRINT" using custom graphics so that there are no lines between the characters.  That's one program that I don't expect to see anyone tackle, as it would be more time consuming then the simple, but quite effective, one-lines that Lance whipped out yesterday.

This is fun!

The Bally Arcade/Astrocade has its fair share of third-party upgrades... all of them quite rare.  One of these upgrades (called "Project 5") was an alternative to the unavailable hi-res mode.  "Project 5" is mentioned in ARCADIAN 5, no. 2 (Dec. 3, 1982): 44.  If you've never heard of this project before... well check out this quote from Mike White's FAQ, "The Bally Astrocade Hardware Guide: Plans, Prototypes and Production (Incorporating Thorough References to the Classic Newsletters):"


PROJECT 5 [plan]  This was to take yet another stab at HI-RES, with the inclusion of an "Extended Color-Graphics Processor Board" containing a TMS9918A Video Display Processor and 16k of RAM!  This would have provided quite a variable resolution over a wide range!  Page 24 of the fifth Arcadian provides its only mention (pricing it at $300.00).


How did you get this proposed upgrade board?  The Arcadian only mentions to "contact me" if you're interested in this project.  "Me," I presume, would have been Bob Fabris.  The person that made these boards (or more likely WOULD make these boards) is never mentioned in the newsletter.  While scanning from "Box 5" of the Fabris collection I came across a letter dated November 16, 1982 from the person that made this information available to Bob.  This person is Rich Tietjens.

Rich Tietjens has several 300-Baud programs available on the BallyAlley.com website.  He may be best known for the elusive "Dungeons And Dragons Program Package" that Paul Thacker was finally able to archive.  I wasn't aware that Rich created hardware projects.  Oh, what information is gleaned from the Bob Fabris Collection!

I scanned the first page of Rich's letter, but the second page is, so far, missing.  I was only able to figure out who wrote the letter using Google.  The clue for me was that the person's address is included in the letter.  I searched the BallyAlley.com website using the zip code included in the address and only came across one match (ARCADIAN 4, no. 4 (Jan. 22, 1982): 44.).  This address happened to be the very same address on the letter's letterhead.  That seemed to be a nice stroke of luck!  Thank you, Google, for your help.

So, what the heck IS the TMS9918A microchip?  It is a Video Display Controller made by Texas Instruments used in a variety of computers, including the well known ColecoVision, MSX range of computers, Sega SG-1000/SC-3000 [the Sega console, not available in the United States, that was available right before the Sega Master System], and the Texas Instruments TI-99/4A (among MANY other less well-known computers).  For more information on this chip read this:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Instruments_TMS9918

So, what would this "Project 5" have been capable of?  The answer to that is in the letter that Rich wrote to Bob:


Dear Bob,

Could you please query the Arcadian subscribers on interest in the following add-on:

Extended color graphics processor board specifications:

Uses TMS9918A Video Display Processor and 16K dynamic RAM (outside Arcade's address space), with 256 x 192 pixel resolution in sixteen colors simultaneously.

Compatible with Blue RAM and other add-on memories (but requires none).

Four display modes:

1.  Multi-color lo-res mode: 48 rows x 64 columns of 4x4 pixel blocks, each of which may be in any of the 16 available colors.

2.  Graphics I - 24 rows x 32 columns of 8x8 pixel character blocks. 256 characters may be user defined in two colors each (all sixteen colors available in the display simultaneously).

3.  Graphics II - similar to Graphics I, but allows 768 different patterns to be defined, each using up to sixteen colors, and 32 "Sprites" are available, each in any one of the sixteen colors. Each sprite is either an 8x8 or 16x16 pixel block, and is moved without the erase-and-redraw procedures needed in the Astrocade.

4.  Text Mode - 24 lines x 40 columns, similar to the Apple II and Atari 400/800 text modes. Each character is defined as a 6x8 pixel block, allowing standard 5x7 characters with normal spacing. Software will be supplied in both 300 and 2000 baud format to display the full ASCII character set, both upper and lower case; up to 256 characters may be defined by the user in each alternate set.

The normal Astrocade display may be shown as a background to the VDP, or hidden with a solid-color "backdrop".

Output is NTSC composite video.

Price is targeted for $300 assembled and tested, including power supply. If there is sufficient demand, a bare board may be made available (but the parts cost is expected to exceed $200 in single quantities).


That's the end of page one of Rich's letter.  The second page of this letter is not in Box 5 of the Fabris Collection, as this letter was found in the last folder that I'm currently scanning.  Perhaps it will turn up elsewhere as I continue to wade through boxes in the future.  Or, maybe this IS the end of the letter?

The setup that Rich proposes (but not the specs) sounds similar to how the planned follow-up of the Magnavox Odyssey 2 would have worked.  That unreleased system would have been called the Odyssey 3 Command Center (in Europe it actually WAS released as the Philips Videopac + G7400).

This is a pretty neat idea, although certainly not realistic price-wise for the time period.  Then again, much of what people were hoping for, like the still unreleased Z-GRASS, would have been drowned by the computer competition at the time.  Yet, I can certainly see how a certain minority of die-hards may have bought this if it actually had been available.  Heck, if someone made it now there would probably be a trickle of them sold.

Any thoughts?

Adam

The Bally Arcade/Astrocade has its fair share of third-party upgrades... all of them quite rare.  One of these upgrades (called "Project 5") was an alternative to the unavailable hi-res mode.  "Project 5" is mentioned in ARCADIAN 5, no. 2 (Dec. 3, 1982): 44.  If you've never heard of this project before... well check out this quote from Mike White's FAQ, "The Bally Astrocade Hardware Guide: Plans, Prototypes and Production (Incorporating Thorough References to the Classic Newsletters):"


PROJECT 5 [plan]  This was to take yet another stab at HI-RES, with the inclusion of an "Extended Color-Graphics Processor Board" containing a TMS9918A Video Display Processor and 16k of RAM!  This would have provided quite a variable resolution over a wide range!  Page 24 of the fifth Arcadian provides its only mention (pricing it at $300.00).


How did you get this proposed upgrade board?  The Arcadian only mentions to "contact me" if you're interested in this project.  "Me," I presume, would have been Bob Fabris.  The person that made these boards (or more likely WOULD make these boards) is never mentioned in the newsletter.  While scanning from "Box 5" of the Fabris collection I came across a letter dated November 16, 1982 from the person that made this information available to Bob.  This person is Rich Tietjens. 

Rich Tietjens has several 300-Baud programs available on the BallyAlley.com website.  He may be best known for the elusive "Dungeons And Dragons Program Package" that Paul Thacker was finally able to archive.  I wasn't aware that Rich created hardware projects.  Oh, what information is gleaned from the Bob Fabris Collection!

I scanned the first page of Rich's letter, but the second page is, so far, missing.  I was only able to figure out who wrote the letter using Google.  The clue for me was that the person's address is included in the letter.  I searched the BallyAlley.com website using the zip code included in the address and only came across one match (ARCADIAN 4, no. 4 (Jan. 22, 1982): 44.).  This address happened to be the very same address on the letter's letterhead.  That seemed to be a nice stroke of luck!  Thank you, Google, for your help.

So, what the heck IS the TMS9918A microchip?  It is a Video Display Controller made by Texas Instruments used in a variety of computers, including the well known ColecoVision, MSX range of computers, Sega SG-1000/SC-3000 [the Sega console, not available in the United States, that was available right before the Sega Master System], and the Texas Instruments TI-99/4A (among MANY other less well-known computers).  For more information on this chip read this:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Instruments_TMS9918

So, what would this "Project 5" have been capable of?  The answer to that is in the letter that Rich wrote to Bob:


Dear Bob,

Could you please query the Arcadian subscribers on interest in the following add-on:

Extended color graphics processor board specifications:

Uses TMS9918A Video Display Processor and 16K dynamic RAM (outside Arcade's address space), with 256 x 192 pixel resolution in sixteen colors simultaneously.

Compatible with Blue RAM and other add-on memories (but requires none).

Four display modes:

1.  Multi-color lo-res mode: 48 rows x 64 columns of 4x4 pixel blocks, each of which may be in any of the 16 available colors.

2.  Graphics I - 24 rows x 32 columns of 8x8 pixel character blocks. 256 characters may be user defined in two colors each (all sixteen colors available in the display simultaneously).

3.  Graphics II - similar to Graphics I, but allows 768 different patterns to be defined, each using up to sixteen colors, and 32 "Sprites" are available, each in any one of the sixteen colors. Each sprite is either an 8x8 or 16x16 pixel block, and is moved without the erase-and-redraw procedures needed in the Astrocade.

4.  Text Mode - 24 lines x 40 columns, similar to the Apple II and Atari 400/800 text modes. Each character is defined as a 6x8 pixel block, allowing standard 5x7 characters with normal spacing. Software will be supplied in both 300 and 2000 baud format to display the full ASCII character set, both upper and lower case; up to 256 characters may be defined by the user in each alternate set.

The normal Astrocade display may be shown as a background to the VDP, or hidden with a solid-color "backdrop".

Output is NTSC composite video.

Price is targeted for $300 assembled and tested, including power supply. If there is sufficient demand, a bare board may be made available (but the parts cost is expected to exceed $200 in single quantities).


That's the end of page one of Rich's letter.  The second page of this letter is not in Box 5 of the Fabris Collection, as this letter was found in the last folder that I'm currently scanning.  Perhaps it will turn up elsewhere as I continue to wade through boxes in the future.  Or, maybe this IS the end of the letter?

The setup that Rich proposes (but not the specs) sounds similar to how the planned follow-up of the Magnavox Odyssey 2 would have worked.  That unreleased system would have been called the Odyssey 3 Command Center (in Europe it actually WAS released as the Philips Videopac + G7400).

This is a pretty neat idea, although certainly not realistic price-wise for the time period.  Then again, much of what people were hoping for, like the still unreleased Z-GRASS, would have been drowned by the computer competition at the time.  Yet, I can certainly see how a certain minority of die-hards may have bought this if it actually had been available.  Heck, if someone made it now there would probably be a trickle of them sold.

Any thoughts?

12189:
Paul Thacker wrote:
>>
[Tietjens Project 5 is] a pretty ambitious plan, though it would need some software
support as well to really be worthwhile.
>>

Right, Project 5 would have needed software support just like a real Hi-Res Unit Astrocade unit would have needed.  If Bally or Astrocade had created a hi-res mode, then software would have had to support it.  One of the very first operations that Bally's on-board ROM does is set low-res mode.  The Home Video Game Library (a group of easy to remember names for ports called HVGLIB.H) shows that port $08 is the output port that sets the Consumer (low-res) or Commercial (Hi-Res) mode.  Here is the equate that is setup in HVGLIB.H:

; INTERRUPT and CONTROL OUTPUT Ports:
CONCM   EQU     $08     ; &(8)= ; write 0 for CONsumer, 1 for CoMmercial mode

Here are the first four operations that the Astrocade performs when turned on:

        NOP                     ; WAIT FOR THINGS TO SETTLE DOWn
        DI
        XOR     A
        OUT     (CONCM),A       ; *** SET CONSUMER MODE ***

For those non-programmers the third line make register A hold a 0 and the fourth line takes that 0 and places it into port $08 (here, called CONCM).

The next thing that the BIOS does is to check if it should run the start-up menu or just begin a cartridge that wants to handle everything in its own way without using the menu (like Bilbrey's "Treasure Cove").  What this means is that no programs ever have to mess with Port $08 because it has been setup as the Astrocade will always require it right from the start.  It's basically "set it and forget it."

Since Low-Res mode is set-up first thing by the On-Board ROM, any program that wishes to use Hi-Res mode would just have to place a 1 into Port $08 and it would now be running in hi-res mode.  If memory serves, if this is done on the Astrocade without it being upgraded, then you just get a blank screen.

On John Perkins Hi-Res unit (in Ken Lill's possession), the low-res screen of the menu only fills 1/4 of the TV's screen.  One of these days soon, I'd like to see Ken build a new power supply for his Hi-Res unit that he has so that the On-Board ROM can be dumped-- as it is the only hi-res program that we have now (well, besides the Arcade games that use the Astrocade chip set).  Or, if the ROM chip isn't soldered, then maybe he can just removed it, dump it, and then replace it in the unit.

>>
there did end up being a decent amount of
software for the Blue RAM, so maybe it could have caught on.
>>

If Tietjens' Hi-Res project had come out, it would have been pretty-late (MUCH later than the Blue Ram-- which shipped in either late 1979 or early 1980).  For the Bally Arcade at that time, the Blue Ram really was an viable, inexpensive upgrade path.  By 1982 this was no longer the case for any hi-res unit (even though people still waited in anticipation for the ZGrass add-on, which actually DIDN'T support hi-res mode).  Still, if it HAD been released, some folks would have adopted it and made some software for Project 5.  Even if they were only demos that basically said, "Look at the potential this hardware has-- why doesn't everyone have it?"

>>
I searched
 the currently scanned documents documents for "Tietjens" and glanced
through the results, but didn't see any more about this.
>>

Eventually the pdfs of the documents in the Bob Fabris Collection will be online and people can do with them what they please.  Since most of the letters are handwritten that information will always be a little difficult to search... except using the old-fashioned, tried and true, serial method way of reading it a letter from start to finish.  I guess, even with the handwritten letters, it's possible that these could be retyped for searching purposes, but I don't imagine that this would ever occur.

12191:
I just finished scanning a small booklet (4 1/2" x 6 3/4") by Tom Wood called "Bally Arcade, Home Video Game, Executive Software Description."  This nineteen page booklet was later released by Cursor as "Bally On-Board ROM Subroutines" with no credit given to Mr. Wood.  Let it be known that Cursor's pages are the EXACT same as Tom's booklet -- but Tom's information is in an easy to carry booklet form.  If there are any changes at all... then I can't find them.  Tom's booklet is small and Cursor's version is on normal 8 1/2" x 11."  This means that Fred Cornett, the editor of Cursor, must have had access to Tom's original pages-- so it would seem that Tom probably allowed this to occur.

It doesn't appear that Cursor did this with everyone else's work, but it's clear that Fred Cornett also took full credit for the "Peek 'n Poke" manual, which was written, via phone conversations, by Brett Bilbrey.  Maybe Tom didn't WANT credit (which is possible).  Or perhaps this missing information about the author is within the pages of the Cursor newsletter (I'm not sure), but it should have also been included within the "Subroutine" and "Peek n' Poke" manuals.

Adam

The Devastator, Devastator II, and the Centurion from us all did.

Our main competitor was Slik Stik and they used Oscar Controls for a while and then made their own-the Tornado. Once I learned what made a spinner, I made our own for the Devastator II and the Centurion. Speaking of Oscar Controls, the company that took over production for us, Arcadegames4U, used Oscar Controls in Devastator II/Centurion sales. Unfortunately, Oscar Controls, with no warning just stopped and disappeared! We almost lost a sale because of it but they managed to get one off of eBay. Arcadegames4U ended up making their own optical boards and their own spinners-not certain if they are available still.

Now, for ones that are. There is NorthCoast Custom Arcades, http://www.mameroom.com/Products_Controllers.asp, and they seem to have gotten permission to make controllers based on Slik Stik designs-and their spinner.

Finally, the other vendor would be Andy Warnes at Ultimarc: and they sell, amongst many other items, the Spin Trak: http://www.ultimarc.com/SpinTrak.html

Best,

James

I've downloaded all of these now.  The letters are probably the most interesting part of this box. 12199:
While going through the Bob Fabris Collection I've seen some pretty neat stuff, most of which I've been able to share so far with the group.  Today I read a letter that an Astrocade user named Murray Greenman in New Zealand (!) sent to Bob in March in 1981.  The letter is just too good to keep to myself... and so I'm attaching it to this posting rather than uploading it to the website.

Murray built himself a computer using a spare Astrocade board that someone that moved to New Zealand brought with them.  He then added everything else required.  For instance, he had no keypad, so he had to add a keyboard.  He had to burn his own BASIC one byte at a time-- talk about a load of work-- this guy was determined!  He built his own BASIC interface using the schematic published in the Arcadian.  He uses a PAL TV (the Astrocade was only designed for use with NTSC TVs), so he gets around that too.  He even makes a crude, but effective, drawing of what his computer looks like too.

I've seen some pretty far-out classic computer systems, and this Bally Arcade system is right up there among the most unusual... and memorable!

Adam
12200:
Ben wrote
>>
I was wondering if anybody has tried the Raspberry Pi with MESS.
>>

I haven't heard anyone here trying MESS with a Pi-- but it has certainly been done before (as I'm sure that you're aware).  For those not in the know who are wondering what IS a Raspberry Pi, it's a small computer that uses an ARM processor in its system on a chip.  The Pi is very small; it's considered "credit card-sized," but since it is so much thicker I don't understand why that is said about it.  The Pi costs either $25 or $35 depending on the model that you get.  Of course, one you hook up other "stuff" to make it usable, then it's price increases (but not drastically).  It has really caught on with hardware hackers.  I first ran into it reading some UK magazines ("Classic Gamer," or "Games," I think).

People use the Pi for neat projects, one of which is using it for playing games and emulators (MAME seems to be popular).  I had never heard of anyone using it with MESS, but I presumed that it was possible and a quick search of Google proved this to be true.  However, I'm not sure how EASY it is to get to grips with.  Ben, whatever you do find out, I'd be quite interested to hear about.

>>
does anybody have
an Astrocade that does not currently work?
>>

That's kind of a loaded question.  If you have an Astrocade, then chances are that you also have another one in the back of a closet or in the garage that doesn't work with plans to get it fixed "one of these days."

>>
I am thinking it would be
kinda cool to build this in an Astrocade case.
>>

Right on!  Dead units (or units with no proof of them working-- that is in an unknown state and sold "as is") go for fairly cheap on Ebay.  I've even seen them not sell at all.  I'm sure that you'll be able to pick one up pretty cheaply.  Using a Pi in an Astrocade case would stop the overheating problem that is so common-- we hope!

Adam

> Instructions from the "Arcadian:"
>
> BIORYTHM by Dave Walter is a version that stores the data for the
three
> graphs outside the program in string locations, and then directs their
> printing in the proper place on the screen. The sine wave is therefore
> quite accurately portrayed. In addition, it is fast moving. To load
the
> string data, load this on tape and save before the program is manually
> loaded:
>
> 10 FOR A=0 TO 86
> 20 PRINT #1 ,"@(",A,")=",
> 30 INPUT @(A)
> 40 NEXT A
>
> After punching in the program, load the string from the tape. The
program is
> now complete. Dump to tape as follows:
>
> :PRINT;LIST;FOR A=0 TO 86;PRINT #1, "@(",A,")=", @(A); NEXT A; PRINT"
> CLEAR;RUN
>
> Then load back to Bally and the program will be self starting.
>
> "Bio-rhythms" has no instructions, but I have gathered this
information from
> the BASIC listing:
>
> The program will ask for the current date and also your birth date. I

In preparation for the release of the "Crazy Climber" ROM imagg, I have released the manual for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade game.  This homebrew game, programmed by Michael Garber, was released in 2012 by Riff Raff Games.  It had a limited run of fifty cartridges.

You can download the manual here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/Crazy%20Climber%20Manual%20(2012)(Riff%20Raff%20Games).pdf

(or use the full URL:)

http://tinyurl.com/a53742c

You would be missing out if you didn't read the full manual in pdf format, but if you'd prefer to read a text version of it, then I have included it below this post.

Enjoy!

Adam


Crazy Climber Manual

Background
----------

Rock climbing and bouldering allow many people to get exercise or thrills.  For Climber, who has climbed nearly as long as he could walk, it is a way of life.  Introduced to the sport by his famous mountain-climbing parents, Climber never lets a day go by without climbing SOMETHING.  He believes that it not only keeps him physically strong and able, but also mentally sharp.  Able to do three consecutive pull-ups using just ONE finger, Climber is more than capable of climbing any rock, cliff face or mountain that nature throws in his direction.  And that is the problem.  Nature can no longer provide anything that Climber can't climb.  A few years ago he began living in large cities so that he could secretly climb the buildings.  Now Climber feels that even the mightiest man-made structures are of little challenge to him.

This morning Climber walked to work through the downtown city streets of his hometown among the towers of iron, glass and concrete.  Where was his next challenge going to come from?  He was deep in thought and nothing was coming to him.  Then, suddenly, there was a loud crash in front of him.  He looked down and there was a potted plant and a shattered container.  He had narrowly missed death!  When Climber looked up he saw that the windows of the building (which he thought could NEVER be opened) were being opened and closed, seemingly at random.  Then he saw a beer bottle coming down at him.  He quickly jumped up and aside.  By instinct, instead of landing on the sidewalk, Climber had tightly clutched the buildings lowest ledge for its shelter and was holding onto it with his fingers...

And then he pulled himself up.  He looked up again and saw people still tossing items out the windows.  He didn't understand what was happening.  Why were these people doing this?  What were they trying to do?  Then it occurred to him.  Perhaps nature couldn't provide a challenge, even the building itself wasn't a challenge to climb, but there was just something about this idea of avoiding these items tossed out by these Crazy, absolutely Mad People that was strangely attractive to him.  Anybody with his ability could climb a building, but could Climber do it AND avoid these Crazy Mad People?

You are about to find out because YOU are Crazy Climber!


Starting the Game
-----------------

1) After inserting the cartridge and turning on the system, choose "CRAZY CLIMBER" by pressing 1 on the keypad or try using the remote game selection by pulling the trigger on hand control #1, turning the knob until 1 appears on the screen, then pulling the trigger again.

2) Pull the Trigger button to pass the Copyright screen.

3) Enter the number of controllers at the "# JOY?" prompt.  You must use the knob to make the selection here.


Playing the Game
----------------

The object of Crazy Climber is to reach the top of a nearly 200-story building.  There are four buildings in total, each offering a variety of different challenges and obstacles that make the journey to the top more difficult.

Crazy Climber's progress is indicated on the right-side of the screen as a blinking dot on a miniature building.  When all of the buildings have been scaled, then Crazy Climber is returned to Building One and play continues at a higher level of difficulty.  The Building Number is indicated by black squares on the top-right side of the screen.

The player has four "Lives" when the game begins and there is NO way to gain an extra "Life," so be careful.  The Number of "Lives" is indicated by green circles on the lower-right side of the screen.

[Screenshot of bottom of first building.]

Crazy Climber Dangers:
----------------------

1) Windows (opening and closing) - If an open window closes on BOTH of Crazy Climber's hands, then he will lose his grip and fall.

2) "Mad People" - These bald-headed scoundrels open and close the windows and drop items out the windows.  They do their very best to knock Crazy Climber off the building.

3) Falling Objects: If a falling object hits Crazy Climber on the head and he is not holding onto a ledge with both hands, then he will fall and lose a "Life."  If he IS holding himself on two ledges, then he will only lose bonus points.  The falling objects are:

1. Flower Pots - Beautiful as they may be, the pots filled with flowers must be avoided.

2. Condor Excrement - Just out of Crazy Climber's sight a condor sometimes flies past.  The condor doesn't attack Crazy Climber, but he does other, perhaps nastier, things.  Avoid his droppings at all cost.  Not only does it cost Crazy Climber a "Life," but it's, well, GROSS.

3. Iron Dumbbells - The flower pots falling down were bad enough, but the "Mad People" eventually step it up and begin to drop out items that REALLY hurt.

4. Falling Bottles - The Mad Potter is always looking for ways to keep Crazy Climber guessing.  He starts rummaging through the garbage and tossing glass bottles out the window when nothing else is within reach.


Scoring
-------

Climbing from ledge to ledge, one floor at a time, and gaining a bonus (at the top of each building) are the only ways to score points.

 Building     Floor Value   Initial Bonus
 --------     -----------   -------------
   1           100 Points      10,000
   2           150 Points      20,000
   3           200 Points      30,000
   4           250 Points      40,000
5 & Higher     250 Points      40,000

The initial level bonus is reduced as Crazy Climber makes his way to the top of the building.  The faster he reaches it, the higher the bonus will be.  The bonus is also reduced by getting hit by falling objects.


Controlling Crazy Climber
-------------------------

The original coin-op of Crazy Climber is played with two controllers allowing the player to easily move Crazy Climber from ledge to ledge.  This is the most natural method to play the game and is offered on the Bally Arcade/Astrocade home version as well.  However, there is no easy method to play and hold the two hand controllers together while at the same time using both of them.  Since this can be difficult, a one-controller version of gameplay is offered.  Both control methods are discussed here:

Two-Controllers
---------------

Crazy Climber's left hand is controlled by the controller in Port 1 and the right hand is controlled by the controller in Port 2.  While this method closely mimics the arcade game's feel, it will take patience to find a way to hold the controllers together.  One recommendation to do this is to place a large pink eraser (it's the perfect size) between the controllers and hold them tightly together with zip ties.

To make Crazy Climber climb the building, move the left and right controllers in opposite vertical directions.  This is the actual motion any climber would take to reach from ledge to ledge.  To move left or right BOTH hands have to be holding onto a ledge.

One-Controller Method (Hand Controller in Port 1)
-------------------------------------------------

To most easily understand how to move Crazy Climber, study this pictogram:

[Pictogram by Ken here.]

With Trigger Pressed: The odd hand is not mirrored when pressing up or down.  The affect of this will be that both hands will eventually be parallel on a ledge.  One common use of this is to "reset" Crazy Climber and get him back to an easier to control, safer starting point.

To get started, wiggle the controller up and down and Crazy Climber will begin to climb the building.

12206:
I'm scanning in a folder from the Bob Fabris collection that is full of Rich
Tietjens letters and programs.  It seems that Bob Fabris used the back of a
couple of menus from a place called "And Chili" located in San Jose,
California.  Normally this would mean nothing to me, but one of the local
Chili's restaurants near our house has one of their old menus up on the
wall-- and this seems to be about the same one.  I couldn't find any
information about Chili's having once been called "And Chili," but I did a
Google search and the same address.  The location on the old menu is
currently the home to a Chili's.  That's probably not a coincidence.

Being a New Mexican, I probably shouldn't say that I even EAT at Chili's, as
there are so many REAL Mexican, New Mexican and Spanish restaurants around
my house (if you're ever in Albuquerque stop by Las Cuates-- or hell, call
me, and we'll go together).  Nowadays a meal at Chili's will usually cost
you about ten bucks (for about the cheapest menu item).  In 1980 (when Bob
used the menu), for $2.50 you could choose from thirteen items.  That's all
the menu consisted of at the time.  Oh, and for $2.50 you could also get
yourself a "Small Pitcher of Margarita or Sangria" (now one margarita costs
about eight bucks).

The Fabris Collection is bringing weird bits of culture together for me.
It's pretty interesting and would make a neat book if someone ever cares to
write it... but I guess they'll need access to the material in the
collection before they can write anything.  Which is why lately I'm trying
to scan a little of it each day.

Adam

Conquering: The Incredible Wizard
December 1982, "Videogaming Illustrated."

The Wizard of Wor comes to home videogaming in Astrocade's finest cartridge
yet.

     Object

     The ancient world is plagued by demons. Some of them are only
moderately annoying; some are utter miseries. Others are positively lethal.
     As a "worrier," it's your task to penetrate the infamous Dungeons of
Wor and rid the land of its many nefarious inhabitants. No problem, you
think. After all, you've an army behind you.
     As soon as you enter the catacombs, you begin to wonder why you ever
volunteered for service. Your knees begin to knock, but you cherish the
feeling for one reason: it means you're still alive.
     Not only are the labyrinths dark and gloomy, eerie sounds creaking and
howling from within, but they are so narrow that only one soldier can
penetrate at a time. It is then that you learn why the king sent a full
battery on this mission: your personnel perish with alarming frequency.
     Your Concentrated Unified Field Disturbance Rifle is fully charged and
you grip it tightly within your perspiring palms. Your radar screen is
operative and you enter the dungeons yourself -- the dungeons where death is
less a question of "if" than a matter of when.
     Your mission is to destroy as many monsters as possible, from Burwors
to Garwors to Thorwors to the great Wizard himself, before your own demise.

     Variations

     There are three levels of play: Easy, Medium, and Hard. The monsters
move with increasing rapidity as the difficulty increases. At the same time
the successive mazes have fewer and fewer walls, permitting the creatures to
come at you from more sides simultaneously. Fortunately, the demons can only
attack vertically and horizontally, never diagonally. In the more open
mazes, you will be distracted by the monsters' approach from all angles: try
to pay their maneuvers no attention, for in the end the creatures can come
at you only from top, bottom, left, or right.

     Scoring

Burwors (blue):           Thorwors (red)
     10 points                 50 points
Garwors (yellow)          The Wizard
     20 points                 250 points
Worluk (blue with yellow wings)
     100 points
Worriors (yellow or blue)
     100 points

     Whenever you destroy a Worluk, the point value of the next maze
doubles. Sizzling the Wizard wins you a quadruple point value. When a Worluk
and Wizard appear in the same maze, failing to destroy one does not affect
your bonus for having eliminated the other. Extra players are awarded every
fourth maze.

     Control

     The Incredible Wizard is fought using Astrocade's three-function
joystick, though only two of the implement's abilities are brought into
play.
     The joystick handle moves your worrior up, down, left, and right, while
he trigger shoots your rifle. A quick jerk to one of those sides will cause
your worrior to face the side without further movement in that direction.
The knob atop the joystick is of no help.

     Patterns

     In time, you will come to recognize some of the mazes. However,
individual patterns do not recur with any regularity. Nor is there any set
place from which the monsters or the Wizard enter the catacombs. However,
they always appear in the same order, the Burwors and Garwors first, and
after a few moments the Thorwors and Worriors.
     The moth-like Worluk flits your way only after all the Wizard's other
familiars have been destroyed; the Wizard comes next, though not all the
time and never after the first maze, but at any time thereafter.
     There is one sure way to tell when the Wizard is about to appear: if
your worrior can discharge more than two shots after the Worluk has been
vanquished or escapes, then the Wizard is on his way. If that is the case,
follow the strategies cited five paragraphs hence.
     Your own worrior always begins by entering through a doorway in the
bottom left of the screen, except in two-player games where the second
participant gets the doorway on the lower right.

     Strategies

     Most of the time, you should blast a monster when you have the chance.
There is little time to reflect on this: the buggers move swiftly! The sole,
incontrovertible exception to shooting-on-sight is when you're gunning down
a
long corridor. At any time, before you can fire a second shot your first one
has to have exploded. If you fire at a remote target and there's a creature
around the corner, your projectile might not reach -- and, hence, you may
not be able to "recharge" -- before the nearer monster arrives and you're
disintegrated.
     As a rule, in any maze try to situate yourself in the corner of a
lengthy tunnel. For the most part, the longest tunnels are horizontal. Not
only will that give you time to turn and fire at whatever is ambling your
way along the
lengthy corridor, there will by virtue of its length be more passageways
leading into that tunnel, ergo more monsters will use it.
     Your only concern beside firing along the tunnel will be to pay
attention to what may be scampering along the short side of the right angle.
The creatures of The Incredible Wizard are quite clever: if they see you
blasting away down the corridor, one or two of them will try to sneak around
and come at you from the side.
     After you have done away with the lesser creatures, the Worluk will
arrive. While the other demons in this game change directions abruptly, none
makes quite so fleet an about-face as the Worluk. With a supernatural
disdain for the laws of physics, it can make immediate, full-speed changes
in its course.
     That means if you've been tailing the Worluk and are close behind it,
you run the very real risk of being run over. At the same time, while it may
very well change direction and head your way, it may stop short of you and
shift gears again. The monster is nothing if mercurial.
     What is predictable is that the Worluk will almost always try to escape
via the door nearest to the spot where it first appeared. Thus, after
clearing the screen of all other menaces, position yourself with a clear
shot at that door. Or, if you want to try and anticipate the Worluk, try to
pick off the winged beast before then. Do this not by chasing it into the
maze, but by nestling at the far end of a long corridor. Moving into the
more convoluted areas of the labyrinth while that devil is buzzing about
will more than likely bring about your ruination.
     The Wizard moves in a manner almost identical to the Worluk, but he has
the added threat of firing projectiles rapidly in all directions. He will
show up more and more frequently the longer you survive.
     Always prepare for the Wizard's arrival by sheltering yourself on as
many sides as possible: this tartar really is a one-man dervish, toting a
pistol as he dashes around the maze, becoming visible for mere moments,
eluding your radar, and changing course unpredictably. After having
determined by the process mentioned above that the Wizard is on his way,
your best bet is to sit in a corner and open fire along a free side, just in
case he happens to materialize there.
     Don't go wandering about: he'll come to you soon enough. Nor should you
vacillate; choose a direction which offers the Wizard the fewest maze walls
in his approach to you, and stay facing that direction. Be prepared,
however, to shift and shoot the other way if he alters his approach.
Further, the Wizard is an exception to the hold-your-fire rule mentioned
earlier. If you don't plug him far down a corridor, his missiles are sure to
nail you.
     Accordingly, even if you don't get the Wizard, make certain he doesn't
get you by never leaving yourself out in the open when he is afoot.
     Another "never-do" applies to every creature in every maze. That is,
never position yourself by the right or left wall near the spot where a
passage leading from one side of the screen to the other opens now and then.
If your back is to the wall when the door appears, and a creature happens
through it on the other side, it will trample you under before you can flee.
     One of the strategies you should always undertake is to shoot clusters
of monsters. You often find two, sometimes three Burwors, Garwors, and/or
Thorwors moving in tandem: at such times, you can obliterate them all with
one shot. If you see a cluster developing, chase it if possible. If one is
already developed, chances are you won't arrive in time to tag them all. The
clusters are extremely short-lived.
     In the more difficult levels, especially "hard," you'll be sitting
still less than in the "easy" level. For one thing, the creatures move
faster; for another, they fire weapons at you. Best to stay on the move,
always firing ahead of yourself to clear a path, pausing to pivot and fire
at any creatures which happen to come at you from another side.
     The most difficult level of all is "The Pit," which has no walls. It is
simply the bare playing field, the monsters, and you. Get yourself at once
to any corner of the field and play from there, shooting vertically or
horizontally as demons approach. Remember, though some of the monsters will
approach from what seems to be a diagonal direction, they must ultimately
have at you from top, bottom, left, or right.
     When it comes time to bag the Worluk, position yourself right before
one of the two exits. It moves so swiftly that, unless you're a
much-decorated Worrior, even a long corridor doesn't give you enough of a
cushion to hit it. Unless your timing is perfect, a missile fired more than
one-third of the screen away from the Worluk will arrive too late to hit it.
And, as mentioned above, trying to anticipate the beast is difficult at
best; in the "hard" level, the difficulty increases geometrically. Which is
a long-winded way of saying that your best bet remains standing by one of
the exits. It must go to one of them . You'll blast the bat-beast if it
heads your way, and be in the ideal position to hit it -- unless it uses the
other side.
     In any maze, if you want an invisible monster to show itself fire in a
"false" direction from the way you want it to come. More often than not the
creature will fall for the bait and attack rather than hide.
     Using the radar to watch those creatures which can become invisible --
all but the Burwors -- is of value solely in the climactic moments of play.
The maze is not indicated on the radar, only the creatures' movements within
the rectangular screen.
     During the thick of battle, when there are many monsters afoot, it's
best to be ready to pivot and blast rather than try to anticipate. The
invisible monsters materialize, literally, a second before they pounce on
you. That's enough time to turn and fire.
     Conversely, if your eyes are on the radar at the bottom of the screen,
you may not have time to interpret its position from the sketchy information
presented on the radar screen, then turn in the right direction. The radar
is best for those times when there is only one Garwor or Thorwor afoot and
you choose to stalk it.

     Comment

     The Incredible Wizard should sell a lot of Astrocade units. Not only is
gameplay superb, and the graphics excellent -- the Wizard's death throes are
dazzling -- but the sound effects are among the best of any home game. There
is music which introduces each maze (if you don't appreciate the delay, cut
the tune short by pressing the trigger), and the six-shooter sounds of the
Wizard's weapon are worth the price of admission.

     Peripheral Vision
     The War Over Wor

     There are going to be some hot times in the marketplace, and it appears
that Astrocade may well be the one taking most of the heat.
     The Incredible Wizard has been on the market for several months now.
Sales-wise, it has done remarkably well considering the fact that Astrocade
still has to overcome several hurdles to make itself felt in the
marketplace.
     One problem is that anyone competing with Atari and Intellivision is
facing a pair of juggernauts. Even monied companies like NAP, which
manufactures Odyssey, have had to work hard to chip away at their lead. What
with Coleco-Vision crowding the marketplace even further, Astrocade has its
work cut out for it.
     Another problem the company has had is a series of name
changes-cum-identity crises over the past few months. They've gone from
being Bally to Astrovision to Astrocade. None of which is to denigrate what
is essentially a very sound game system.
     Nor do Astrocade's difficulties end there. A new specter has arisen,
one which attacks The Incredible Wizard specifically: the new CBS games unit
is making ready to release the same game under its original arcade title,
The Wizard of Wor. The CBS game will be Atari-compatible.
     Just how Midway, which produced the arcade version, licensed the game
to two companies is not clear at present, though we'll have the story for
you next issue.
     What's clear is that CBS, with an aggressive campaign, very slick
packaging, and the benefit of being available in a format which can be used
with the most popular home videogame unit of them all, might well be a
greater foe than any fought by the Astrocade Wizard on the TV screen.

I hadn't figured that the license had expired.  I thought that the answer

Atari 2600 - CBS Electronics
Atari 5200 - CBS Electronics
Atari 8-bit - Roklan Roklan Corp.
Bally Arcade/Astrocade - Astrocade, Inc.
Commodore 64 - Commodore
Commodore Max - Commodore (Runs on C64 but is FAR less impressive)

the short list that I could come with off the top of my head), but checking
Wikipedia I find that these are also the only systems listed.  Not that
Wikipedia is always to be tried and trusted (it doesn't even list the Max
version).

Does anyone else know of other Wizard of Wor ports besides those listed?

ported by another company) or maybe it was released in Japan (well, I guess
the Max version covers that area).  There was supposed to be a Colecovision
release, but it never happened (and I can't recall an available prototype
ROM of it).

Besides the Astrocade version of "Wizard of Wor," I think that my favorite
port is the Atari 8-Bit version, which is very similar to the C64 port that
I grew up with (and used to play quite a bit, actually).
